metadata.title: One Script, Not One Call Each.
metadata.subtitle: The Weekly-Report Skill (One Script vs. Per-SKU Calls)
metadata.purpose: Take the weekly-report skill apart in the Teardown register: explain why the whole report comes out of one script run once, not a tool call per SKU; expose the design trade-off (one round-trip through the data at the cost of a per-row conversation); and show how the same skill splits into a shorter daily sweep. Lands the carry-out that Claude reads every row once instead of checking SKU by hand, and that which sections print still depends on whether the ask was the full weekly review or the shorter daily sweep.

beats.narration_text: The wrong guess: Claude calls one tool per SKU to build this report. It doesn't — the whole report comes out of a single tool call. So the real question is: how does one call cover a file with tens of thousands of rows?

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. A skill is a folder Claude reads before it acts. This one — weekly-report — carries a SKILL.md that names four sections it always prints: stockouts, low stock, open purchase orders, forecast risk. It also binds each section to its file: a stock-levels file, a products file, a sales-history file, an open-orders file. The design choice worth naming: the layout is handed to Claude up front, so nothing has to be guessed at runtime.

production_viz.label: A SKILL IS A FOLDER
production_viz.caption: SKILL.md names the files and the sections

beats.narration_text: The rule inside is explicit: write one script and run it once. The stock file alone carries about sixty-seven thousand rows — a tool-per-SKU pattern would burn sixty-seven thousand round trips on a report you want in one. So one script loads every file, computes stockouts and days of cover across all of them together, and prints the finished report in a single pass. They optimized for one round-trip through the data; the cost is you never see a per-row conversation. What the report actually contains still depends on the ask: the weekly version adds an aging check — any open purchase order older than its supplier's usual lead time gets flagged — while the daily sweep drops open orders and forecast risk, and leads with whatever action was already taken.

beats.narration_text: Ask Claude for this report and it writes one script that reads every row once — not one tool call per SKU. Which sections that script prints still depends on the ask: the full weekly review, or the shorter daily sweep.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Give it a made-up inventory setup — a stock-levels file with about sixty thousand rows and a separate purchase-orders file — and ask: would you check this row by row with tool calls, or write one script that computes the whole weekly report in one pass? Have it walk you through what that script would need to read, and what the top of the report would say. Go deeper: then ask it to rewrite the same skill for the daily sweep — which sections drop, which section leads, and what that split reveals about the design choice behind separating weekly from daily.

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm designing an Anthropic skill for a weekly inventory report. I have a stock-levels file with about 60,000 rows and a separate purchase-orders file. Would you check this row by row with tool calls, or write one script that computes the whole weekly report — stockouts, low stock, open orders, and which orders are aging past their supplier's lead time — in a single pass? Walk me through what that script would need to read, and show me what the top of the report would say.
